title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 63–64
description: Advanced distinctions in silence, sound verbs and acoustic intensity, followed by precise adjectives and verb patterns for weight and physical or figurative density.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study based on the user-provided textbook. Vocabulary targets follow the study pages, exercises and answers; all explanations, translations, usage notes and sample sentences are newly written. Source exercises, extended passages, tables and illustrations are not reproduced.

units.title: Unit 63 — Sounds: listen up!
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 132–133 (PDF pages 134–135).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · sound, silence and acoustic descriptions
learningObjectives: Distinguish silent, quiet, noiseless and soundless across natural contexts and registers.
Choose precise sound verbs for doors, machinery, music, sirens, cooking and collisions.
Describe unusual silence and unpleasant or extreme sounds using appropriate adjectives.
Understand fixed expressions about silence, excessive noise and the need for quiet.

sectionsChecked: A · Adjectives indicating lack of sound and their collocations
B · Verbs for describing specific noises
C · Some adjectives for noise and silence
D · Fixed expressions connected with noise and silence

items.example: The audience fell silent as the final speaker approached the microphone.
items.note: Silent implies no speech or sound, sometimes when sound might be expected.

items.example: We chose a quiet café where we could discuss the proposal.
items.note: Quiet suggests little noise or activity, not necessarily complete silence.

items.example: The new ventilation system is virtually noiseless.
items.note: Often used of machinery or movement that produces very little or no audible noise.

items.example: The technician stepped noiselessly into the dark laboratory.
items.note: Adverb of noiseless; tends to sound formal or literary.

items.example: The security footage showed the incident in a soundless sequence.
items.note: Suggests an absence of sound, sometimes surprisingly; soundlessly is especially common in descriptions.

items.example: The drone vanished soundlessly behind the trees.
items.note: Formal or literary adverb used for movement without an expected sound.

items.example: The festival screened a restored silent film with live piano accompaniment.
items.note: A film made without synchronised recorded dialogue, especially from early cinema.

items.pt: dia tranquilo; dia de pouco movimento
items.example: The reception team had a quiet day because hardly anyone visited the office.
items.note: Quiet can describe low activity as well as low noise.

items.example: The students held a silent protest outside the main administration building.
items.note: A demonstration without chanting or speaking; highlighted in exercise 63.1.

items.pt: bater com força; fechar com estrondo
items.example: A gust of wind slammed the laboratory door against its frame.
items.note: Often of a door closing abruptly with a loud bang.

items.example: The trolley wheels squeaked whenever the cart turned sharply.
items.note: A short, high-pitched sound, often caused by friction.

items.pt: retumbar; bater de forma repetitiva e forte
items.example: Heavy bass notes pounded through the apartment wall until dawn.
items.note: Of music or other repeated sounds, a heavy rhythmic beating.

items.example: The timber staircase creaked beneath our feet.
items.note: Often of old wood or a joint under pressure.

items.example: Fresh vegetables sizzled in the hot oil as the chef prepared dinner.
items.note: Characteristic continuous sound of food frying.

items.example: A single alarm bell rang out across the empty factory.
items.note: A clear or sudden loud sound, often a bell, shot or shout.

items.example: Waves crashed against the sea wall during the storm.
items.note: A loud heavy impact sound; especially natural with waves and collisions.

items.example: A driver hooted impatiently as the queue began to move.
items.note: In the unit, used of a vehicle horn; also describes the sound of an owl.

items.example: The delivery driver tooted twice before leaving the driveway.
items.note: Typically a short, comparatively light horn sound; less forceful than hoot.

items.pt: uivar; emitir som longo e lamentoso
items.example: The emergency siren wailed across the neighbourhood.
items.note: A high, often rising-and-falling sound; also used of people crying loudly.

items.pt: bater repetidamente e com força em
items.example: Someone hammered at the front door until the neighbours answered.
items.note: Hammer at a door means knock very forcefully and repeatedly.

items.example: The metal hatch slammed shut behind the workers.
items.note: Common pattern describing something closing suddenly with force.

items.example: The pounding music made it difficult to concentrate on the instructions.
items.note: Emphasises a repeated heavy beat that can be heard or felt.

items.example: The sound of a police siren grew louder as the vehicle approached.
items.note: Sirens typically wail, producing a prolonged changing pitch.

items.example: An eerie stillness settled over the abandoned shopping centre.
items.note: Creates an unsettling, almost frightening atmosphere, especially with silence.

items.example: An eerie silence followed the sudden power failure.
items.note: A lack of sound that feels unnatural or unsettling.

items.example: The engine test produced a deafening roar despite the protective enclosure.
items.note: Extremely loud, potentially uncomfortable or painful.

items.example: The presenter had a grating voice that distracted from an interesting topic.
items.note: A harsh, unpleasant sound or voice that irritates the listener.

items.example: A piercing alarm cut through the noise of the workshop.
items.note: A very sharp, high sound that seems to hurt the ears.

items.example: The faulty bearing produced a high-pitched whine.
items.note: Refers to pitch rather than volume; a high-pitched sound is not necessarily loud.

items.example: A faint ticking could still be heard beneath the cooling fan.
items.note: A sound that is weak or difficult to hear, but remains audible.

items.example: The final words of the announcement were inaudible from the back row.
items.note: Cannot be heard, unlike faint, which may still be heard with effort.

items.word: you could have heard a pin drop
items.pt: dava para ouvir uma agulha cair; silêncio absoluto
items.example: After the unexpected verdict, you could have heard a pin drop.
items.note: Idiomatic comment on complete silence, often because everyone is listening or shocked.

items.pt: não consigo nem pensar de tanto barulho
items.example: Please lower the volume; I can't hear myself think.
items.note: A conventional complaint about noise so loud that concentration is difficult.

items.example: We went to the countryside for some peace and quiet after a demanding month.
items.note: A common fixed pairing for calm surroundings without disturbance.

items.pt: silencioso como um ratinho; extremamente quieto
items.example: The usually energetic child was as quiet as a mouse during the performance.
items.note: Simile for someone making almost no noise; typically said as quiet as a mouse.

units.title: Unit 64 — Weight and density
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 134–135 (PDF pages 136–137).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Basic concepts · heaviness, density and physical or figurative weight
learningObjectives: Select precise alternatives to heavy according to physical and figurative context.
Use weigh phrasal verbs with correct particles and distinguish their separate meanings.
Describe thickening, thinning, sifting, solidification and dilution accurately.
Recognise literal and metaphorical meanings of impenetrable, impervious and lightweight.

sectionsChecked: A · Synonyms for heavy: collocation contexts
C · Making things more or less dense

items.example: The committee spent the afternoon considering several weighty ethical questions.
items.note: Can describe a physically heavy book or a serious, important abstract matter.

items.pt: difícil de manusear; pouco prático; complicado
items.example: The legacy database became unwieldy as more services depended on it.
items.note: Large or complex and difficult to manage, physically or organisationally.

items.pt: volumoso e pouco prático; complicado de operar
items.example: The old calibration procedure was too cumbersome for routine use.
items.note: Often of equipment, processes or systems that are awkward to handle or use.

items.pt: oneroso; pesado em termos de obrigação
items.example: Frequent reporting requirements became burdensome for the small research team.
items.note: Normally figurative: imposes a heavy responsibility, cost or obligation.

items.pt: pesado e lento; maçante; excessivamente solene
items.example: His ponderous explanation made a straightforward concept sound complicated.
items.note: Slow, clumsy or over-serious; particularly of speech, writing and arguments.

items.pt: pesado e desajeitado ao se mover
items.example: A lumbering vehicle crossed the uneven ground beside the site.
items.note: Suggests visibly large, heavy, clumsy movement; usually physical rather than abstract.

items.pt: questão séria; assunto de grande importância
items.example: Data privacy became a weighty issue during the product review.
items.note: Weighty adds gravity and importance, rather than literal weight.

items.pt: processo burocrático ou difícil de executar
items.example: A cumbersome approval process delayed the installation for several weeks.
items.note: A process with too many awkward, time-consuming steps.

items.pt: estilo pesado; estilo de escrita maçante
items.example: The reviewer suggested simplifying the article’s ponderous style.
items.note: Describes over-elaborate or solemn prose that is hard to read.

items.example: The extra equipment weighed the hikers down on the steep path.
items.note: Can refer to a physical load or to psychological burdens; often used in the passive.

items.example: The supervisor seemed weighed down with administrative responsibilities.
items.note: A common passive construction, followed by the source of the burden.

items.example: We need to weigh up the advantages and risks before changing the design.
items.note: Weigh up something means carefully compare alternatives or considerations.

items.example: The baker weighed out the flour for each batch.
items.note: Used when measuring a specified quantity of loose material or goods.

items.example: The unresolved complaint continued to weigh on the manager.
items.note: Of guilt or worries that trouble someone over time; often weigh on someone’s mind.

items.pt: intervir em uma discussão; dar uma opinião enfática
items.example: The legal adviser weighed in after the technical team had outlined the options.
items.note: Add an opinion or argument, often forcefully; weigh in with an argument is common.

items.pt: não sair da cabeça; causar preocupação persistente
items.example: The uncertain funding decision had been weighing on her mind all week.
items.note: A figurative expression for a concern that occupies your thoughts.

items.pt: engrossar; tornar mais espesso ou denso
items.example: The fog thickened rapidly as the temperature dropped.
items.note: Make or become thicker; applies to liquids, hair, fog and figurative situations.

items.example: Sift the flour before mixing it with the other dry ingredients.
items.note: Shake a powder or granular substance through a sieve.

items.example: The sauce can go lumpy if you add the starch too quickly.
items.note: Describes the formation of small solid lumps in a mixture.

items.example: The fat had congealed on the surface of the cold broth.
items.note: A liquid or semi-liquid becomes thick or solid, often as it cools.

items.example: The molten material began to solidify inside the mould.
items.note: Become solid, rather than merely thicker.

items.example: Thin the varnish according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
items.note: As a verb, make a liquid less thick; also describes making a group less dense.

items.example: The fog gradually thinned out as the sun rose.
items.note: Make or become less dense; used of fog, crowds, hair or traffic.

items.example: Dilute the cleaning solution before applying it to the surface.
items.note: Reduce the strength or concentration of a liquid by adding water or another liquid.

items.example: The team watered down the proposal to make it acceptable to more reviewers.
items.note: Literally add water; figuratively weaken a plan, argument or statement.

items.example: The instructions warn against using the detergent undiluted.
items.note: Without dilution; especially relevant to instructions and concentrations.

items.pt: desbastar o cabelo; reduzir o volume do cabelo
items.example: The stylist used special scissors to thin out her very thick hair.
items.note: Transitive pattern for reducing hair volume; discussed in the teaching text and tested in the exercises.

items.example: Traffic finally began to thin out after the evening rush hour.
items.note: Applied to a group becoming less dense as numbers decrease.

items.pt: impenetrável; impossível de atravessar ou compreender
items.example: Thick thorn bushes formed an impenetrable barrier around the garden.
items.note: Literally impossible to pass through; figuratively impossible to understand.

items.example: The report buried its useful conclusions beneath impenetrable jargon.
items.note: Figuratively describes language too dense or obscure to understand.

items.example: The protective coating is impervious to water under normal conditions.
items.note: Literally does not allow a substance to pass through; typically impervious to.

items.pt: imune a críticas; indiferente a críticas
items.example: Despite repeated warnings, the director remained impervious to criticism.
items.note: Figuratively unaffected or unmoved by criticism or persuasion; keep to.

items.example: The scientific paper was dense but carefully argued.
items.note: Dense can mean closely packed, or figuratively complex and difficult to digest.

items.example: Dense fog reduced visibility on the motorway early in the morning.
items.note: A natural collocation for fog so thick that visibility is poor.

items.example: Several reviewers dismissed the policy analysis as lightweight.
items.note: Exercise-only figurative contrast: lacking seriousness or intellectual substance.
